system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-02-23 09:50:00 to 2187-02-25 21:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with recurrent primary central nervous system B-cell lymphoma was admitted electively for his 27th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. Admission labs revealed a persistently low white blood cell count (2.7), which contraindicated chemotherapy due to infection risk. The cause was unclear but likely related to prior treatment or possible bone marrow involvement. He remained on Keppra for seizure control and was started on lamotrigine for improved prophylaxis. Airborne precautions were initiated due to a positive PPD and family history of TB but discontinued after a chest X-ray showed only old granulomatous changes without active disease. He was discharged home with instructions to continue all home medications, monitor for rash on lamotrigine, and attend an outpatient bone marrow biopsy to evaluate the cause of leukopenia before resuming chemotherapy.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Osteoarthrosis, unspecified whether generalized or localized, site unspecified
Essential and other specified forms of tremor
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

procedures.long_title: Injection or infusion of cancer chemotherapeutic substance

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, your neurology team doctor. You're here today for your 27th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy for your CNS lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, I’ve been preparing for this. I finished my last dose of temozolomide this week as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve been through induction, maintenance, and re-induction therapy. This is your scheduled two-month interval dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling okay—no headaches, seizures, or balance issues. I was worried because last time they had to send me home over low white blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. The note mentioned increased alcohol use may have contributed. Your labs today show your WBC is 5.2, which is within safe range. So we can proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve cut back completely. I want to stay on track with treatment. My mom’s not doing well, but I decided to wait to visit until after this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a wise decision. We’ll get you through this cycle safely. We’ll also do an EEG today to monitor your seizure risk, since you’ve had seizures in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the last seizure—it caused that fall and the cut on my forehead. I’m still on Keppra, 1000 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levetiracetam is helping. The EEG will help us see if there’s any ongoing brain activity that might increase seizure risk, especially near your prior tumor site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I’m a bit nervous about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s completely painless. Small sensors go on your scalp. You just need to stay still and maybe do some deep breathing. We won’t do hyperventilation because of your brain surgery history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. When will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The report may not be final until after discharge, but we’ll review it at your follow-up. For now, we’re focused on getting your chemotherapy in safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just completed the infusion of high-dose methotrexate at 8 grams per square meter. Everything went smoothly. No reactions during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How long until it’s out of my system?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood levels. You’ll need leucovorin to 'rescue' your healthy cells from the chemo. We’ll start that tomorrow and continue after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s like an antidote, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We also give sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys and lots of fluids to help flush the drug out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll drink plenty when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level yesterday was 4.9, which is expected after the infusion. Today’s level is down to 0.17—excellent. That means it’s clearing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want you to take a few doses of leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate here first to make sure you’re stable. You’ll continue them at home for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I don’t miss any doses. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual medications continue—Desmopressin for diabetes insipidus, lisinopril for blood pressure, and Keppra for seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Lamictal? I’m on 25 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing that to 50 mg twice a day. It’s an extra anti-seizure medication, and we want to keep building protection, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll watch for any rash, like they told me last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s rare but important. If you see any rash, stop it and call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have a preliminary note on your EEG. It showed mild slowing in the left central temporal area, which is near your prior tumor and surgery site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Does it mean I’m going to have another seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It just shows some ongoing irritation or scar tissue in that area. The good news is no epileptiform discharges—those are the patterns that strongly predict seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the Keppra and Lamictal are doing their job?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that’s why we’re keeping you on both. You’ve been seizure-free, and we want to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your white blood cell count dropped to 3.4, which is a bit low but expected after chemo. It’s not dangerously low, and it should recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not surprised. I just hope I don’t get sick. Should I avoid crowds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, good idea. Avoid large groups, wash your hands, and watch for fever. Call us if you hit 100.4 or higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is now 0.17, low enough for safe discharge. You’ve completed the critical part of the protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take leucovorin 40 mg every six hours for three days, sodium bicarbonate twice a day, and drink extra fluids. Continue all your regular meds, including the increased Lamictal dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. Lee next week to review the final EEG and plan your next steps. We’ll decide then about future chemo cycles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care. I’ll follow the instructions carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done very well. Stay hydrated, rest, and call us with any concerns. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder—your discharge meds include leucovorin, sodium bicarbonate, and the updated Lamictal dose. The pharmacy will have them ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got my list. I’ll double-check everything before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—because of your mother’s history of TB and your positive PPD, you’re at higher risk. But no signs of active infection. Just stay alert for cough or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they started INH before, but it affected my liver with chemo. Not on it now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re not restarting it now due to liver concerns. We’ll reassess at follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Nurse will give you final instructions and your medication packets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to go. I’ll take good care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One final check-in. How are you feeling? Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. A little tired, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s normal. Just rest when you get home. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve received all discharge instructions, medications, and follow-up details?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s clear. I’ve got my meds, the schedule, and the appointment. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note before discharge: your condition is stable, mental status clear, and you’re ambulatory. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll follow all the instructions. See you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Call us with any issues. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old man with primary central nervous system B-cell lymphoma was admitted electively for his 27th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. His white blood cell count had previously been low due to increased alcohol use, but it had recovered to a safe level for treatment. The chemotherapy infusion was completed without complications. An EEG was performed during admission, showing mild focal slowing in the left temporal region consistent with prior brain surgery and tumor site, but no epileptiform discharges. Methotrexate levels were monitored and decreased appropriately, allowing for safe discharge. The patient was instructed to continue leucovorin and sodium bicarbonate for three days post-discharge, increase lamotrigine to 50 mg twice daily for seizure prophylaxis, and follow up with his oncologist to review EEG results and plan future therapy. He was discharged home in stable condition.
